old: GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Ltd is the developer. The airport is at Bhogapuram, Vizianagaram district, costs ₹4,750 crore and has a Phase I capacity of 60 lakh passengers per year.
new: GMR Visakhapatnam International Airport Ltd is the developer. The airport is at Bhogapuram, Vizianagaram district, costs over ₹5,640 crore and has a capacity of about 60 lakh (6 million) passengers per year.

old: JSW’s integrated steel plant is at Kadapa; KIA is at Anantapur, Royal Enfield near Tirupati and the DRDO AMCA centre at Puttaparthi.
new: JSW’s integrated steel plant is at Kadapa; the KIA plant is at Penukonda in Sri Sathya Sai district (earlier Anantapur), Royal Enfield near Tirupati and the DRDO AMCA centre at Puttaparthi.

old: Sarcophagi are more common in Chittoor and Anantapur, and one was found near Nallavaram. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
new: Sarcophagus (terracotta coffin) burials are linked with Nagarjunakonda and the Krishna valley, not Visakhapatnam. Anthropomorphic megaliths are in the Tirupati region, menhirs in Krishna, and dolmens in Krishna, Chittoor and East Godavari, so those pairs are correct.

old: Stupa No. 3 holds relics of the Buddha's disciples Sariputra and Mudgalayana; Stupa No. 2 holds relics of monks of the Ashokan missionary era.
new: Stupa No. 3 at Sanchi holds relics of the Buddha's disciples Sariputra (Sariputta) and Mudgalayana (Moggallana).

old: The Hathigumpha inscription in the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves of Odisha records Kharavela's reign year by year; it belongs to the 2nd century BC.
new: The Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri, near Bhubaneswar, records Kharavela's reign year by year; it belongs to the 2nd century BC.

old: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription is in the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves of Odisha. The Nanaghat inscription belongs to the Satavahana queen Naganika, so pairing it with Rudradaman or Kharavela is wrong, and Naganika has nothing to do with Hathigumpha.
new: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription is at Udayagiri near Bhubaneswar. The Nanaghat inscription belongs to the Satavahana queen Naganika, so pairing it with Rudradaman or Kharavela is wrong, and Naganika has nothing to do with Hathigumpha.

old: The Shungas ruled from about 185 BCE, when Brihadratha was killed, to about 73 BCE, when Vasudeva Kanva killed Devabhuti.
new: The Sungas ruled from the killing of Brihadratha (187 BC in the notes, often given as about 185 BCE) until Vasudeva Kanva killed Devabhuti (about 75-73 BCE). So 185 BCE-73 BCE is the closest option.

old: Indravarma, who ruled from 358 to 370 CE, is described as the founder of the Vishnukundin dynasty and a Vakataka vassal.
new: Indravarma was the founder of the Vishnukundin dynasty and a vassal of the Vakatakas. He built Indrapalanagara.

old: Madhava Varma I is credited with the Undavalli, Bhairavakonda and Mogalrajapuram caves in the attribution followed by APP and CDX.
new: Madhava Varma I of the Vishnukundins is credited with the Undavalli, Bhairavakonda and Mogalrajapuram caves.

old: APP and CDX credit Madhava Varma I, while APHQ dates the caves to the Pallava period of the 7th-8th centuries CE.
new: Some historians credit the Bhairavakonda caves to the Vishnukundin ruler Madhava Varma I. Others date them to the Pallava period (7th-8th c. CE).

old: Charles Masson described the ruins during 1826-38; Fleet published seals in 1912 and Sahni found Harappa in 1921-22.
new: Charles Masson first reported the Harappa mounds in 1826 and described the ruins during 1826-38. J. Fleet published Harappan seals in 1912, and Daya Ram Sahni found Harappa in 1921.

old: Lothal's excavation began in 1954; 1931 is the year for Chanhudaro. Harappa (1921) and Mohenjodaro (1922) are correct.
new: Lothal was found by S. R. Rao in 1954 (dug 1955-60), so 'Lothal - 1931' is wrong; 1931 belongs to Chanhudaro. Harappa (1921) and Mohenjodaro (1922) are correctly matched.

old: Differences in house size, burial goods and ornaments indicate social stratification; the four-fold division is speculative.
new: Differences in house size and grave goods point to social stratification in the IVC.

old: Gudimallam is described as having the oldest Shaivite temple in Andhra Pradesh and as representing the first Shiva lingam in Andhra Pradesh and India in the cited tradition.
new: Gudimallam in Chittoor district, of the Satavahana era, has the oldest Shiva lingam and Shaivite temple in Andhra Pradesh.

old: The Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase is identified in the table with Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP).
new: The Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase of the Late Harappan culture, in Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, is marked by Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP).

old: The horse was central to Rigvedic, not Harappan, warfare; Harappan cultural transmission is associated with seals and script.
new: The Harappans had no horse-drawn chariots, so that pair is wrong; chariots, coat of mail and helmet belong to Rigvedic warfare. Harappan settlements were urban and planned, and the Rigvedic horse was domesticated and central to warfare.

old: Mayiladumparai (Krishnagiri district, Tamil Nadu) is AMS-dated to 2172 BCE and is described as the earliest iron-use evidence in India. Sivagalai (Thoothukudi) is the site with iron dated to about 2953 BCE, Thirumalapuram (Tenkasi) has an Iron Age urn chamber, and Adichanallur is the type-site for urn burials.
new: Mayiladumparai in Krishnagiri district has iron AMS-dated to 2172 BCE, the earliest claim before Sivagalai. Sivagalai (Thoothukudi) is now the oldest at about 2953 BCE; Thirumalapuram (Tenkasi) has an Iron Age urn chamber and Adichanallur has urn burials.

old: Bimbisara (544-492 BCE) is treated as the founder of the Haryanka dynasty (APPSC-GS 2018, BPSC 2024). Ajatashatru and Udayin were his Haryanka successors, while Shishunaga founded the next dynasty.
new: Bimbisara (544-492 BCE) founded the Haryanka dynasty of Magadha. Ajatashatru and Udayin were his Haryanka successors, while Shishunaga founded the next dynasty.

old: Gold coins in large number came with the Kushanas (1st-2nd c. CE). Before them the earliest coins were silver punch-marked coins (c. 6th-5th c. BCE), used under the Haryankas, Nandas and Mauryas.
new: The Kushanas (1st–2nd c. CE) were the first to issue gold coins in large numbers. Before them, India's coins were mostly silver punch-marked coins (7th–6th c. BC to the Mauryan period), issued under the Haryankas, Nandas and Mauryas.

old: Erragudi is in Andhra Pradesh, not Karnataka; Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra are in Pakistan and Kandahar in Afghanistan.
new: Erragudi (Yerragudi), with Major and Minor Rock Edicts, is in Andhra Pradesh. It is now in Nandyal district, earlier part of Kurnool district.

old: Tilapishaka were oil-pressers; Kolika were weavers, Padhika butchers and Udayantrika makers of water-machines.
new: Tilapishaka (Tailika) were the oil-pressers' guild. Kolika were weavers, Kulara potters and Udayantrika makers of water-machines; butchers were Katika.

old: Brihatkatha formed the basis of Kathasaritsagara by Somadeva Suri and Brihatkatha Manjari by Kshemendra.
new: Kshemendra wrote the Brihatkatha Manjari, a Sanskrit version of Gunadhya's Brihatkatha. The other Sanskrit version, the Kathasaritsagara, is by Somadeva of Kashmir, not the Jain Somadeva Suri.

old: Colin Mackenzie is identified as the first Director General of the Survey of India.
new: Colin Mackenzie, who identified Amaravati in 1797, was the first Surveyor General of India.

old: Siddharthaka chaitya is associated with Guntupalli, not Nagarjunakonda. Dhanyakataka, Vijayapuri and Kantakasala are respectively associated with Amaravati-Dharanikota, Nagarjunakonda and Ghantasala.
new: Siddharthaka chaitya is at Gudivada (G2 2008 key), not Nagarjunakonda. Kantakasala = Ghantasala, Vijayapuri = Nagarjunakonda and Dhanyakataka = Amaravati-Dharanikota are correct.

old: The Siddharthika sect was centred at Gudivada; do not confuse it with the Siddharthaka chaitya at Guntupalli.
new: The Siddharthika sect was centred at Gudivada; the Siddharthaka chaitya is also at Gudivada. Guntupalli was the Rajagirika centre.

old: Dhanyakataka was the main centre of the Mahasanghika sect. Rajagirika was associated with Sriparvatam and Bhadrayaniya with Nasik.
new: Dhanyakataka was the main centre of the Mahasanghika sect. Rajagirika was centred at Guntupalli (G2 2012 key) and Bhadrayaniya at Nasik, so the other pairs are wrong.

old: Vogel proposed a Kannada origin. Rapson and Buhler held a North Indian origin, D.R. Bhandarkar a Kshatriya or mixed origin and Gopalachari a Telugu/Andhra origin.
new: Vogel proposed a Kannada origin. Rapson and Buhler held a North Indian origin, D.R. Bhandarkar a Kshatriya or mixed Kshatriya-Brahmin origin, and the Telugu/Andhra origin is Caldwell's view (Gopalachari suggested Tamil links).

old: Vogel proposed a Kannada origin; Rapson and Buhler a North Indian one; Gopalachari a Telugu one.
new: Vogel proposed a Kannada origin. Rapson and Buhler held a North Indian origin, Caldwell a Telugu origin, and Gopalachari suggested Tamil links.

old: Kushanas and Sakas paid homage, while kings of Southeast Asia and Ceylon sent tribute.
new: The Kushanas and Sakas were among the distant powers, with Sri Lanka and South-East Asia, that accepted Samudragupta's suzerainty and paid him homage.

old: Samudragupta ruled approximately from 335 to 375 CE. Ghatotkacha belonged to c. 280–319 CE, Chandragupta I to 319–335 CE, and Chandragupta II to about 380–413 CE.
new: Samudragupta ruled c. 335–375 CE. Ghatotkacha ruled c. 280–319 CE, Chandragupta I 319–335 CE and Chandragupta II c. 380–415 CE, so the other pairs are wrong.

old: The Gwalior inscription belongs to Mihirakula's rule. Sondani belongs to Yashodharman, the Maukhari seal to Sarvavarman and the Chausath Yogini inscription to Devapala.
new: The Gwalior inscription shows Mihirakula's rule over Gwalior. The Sondani (Mandasor) pillars record Yashodharman's defeat of Mihirakula, and the Maukhari copper seal belongs to Sarvavarman, not Yashodharman.

old: Vishti was forced labour and was treated as a form of tax; tax-free land went to Brahmins and religious functionaries.
new: Vishti was forced, unpaid labour for the army, officials or the state. It was treated as a source of state income, a kind of tax.

old: Fa-Hien was in India c. 399-414 CE, in the reign of Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya), though he never named the king. Samudragupta ruled before this; Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta ruled after it.
new: Fa-Hien was in India c. 399–412 CE, in the reign of Chandragupta II, though he never named the king. Samudragupta ruled before this; Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta ruled after it.

old: The Mother and Child panel is in Cave 17; Padmapani and Vajrapani are Bodhisattvas.
new: The Mother and Child panel is in Ajanta Cave 17, which also has the Bhava-chakra (wheel of life).

old: The Madhuban plate is useful for Harsha's chronology, alongside the Sonpat seal and the Banskhera inscription.
new: The Madhuban plate is a land-grant record that, with the Sonpat seal, helps fix the chronology of Harsha's reign. The Banskhera inscription is the one that bears Harsha's signature.

old: The order is Dashavatara, Ravan ki Khai, Dumar Lena and then Kailasa, so Kailasa is the latest of the four.
new: The order is Ravan ki Khai, Dumar Lena, Dashavatara and then Kailasa, so Kailasa (Cave 16, Krishna I) is the latest of the four.

old: The APPSC-GS 2018 key gives the Marturu inscription. The Aihole inscription is Ravikirti's prasasti and the Satara inscription records Kubja Vishnuvardhana's appointment to Vengi.
new: The Marturu (Maruturu) inscription of Pulakesin II calls Mangalagiri 'Mangalapura' (APPSC-GS 2018 key), not Kopparam. The Aihole inscription is Ravikirti's prasasti and the Satara inscription records Kubja Vishnuvardhana's appointment to Vengi.

old: Tribhuvanankusa was the seal sign manual; the emblem was the boar, the matronymic Hariti-putra and the mother goddess Kushmandini.
new: Tribhuvanankusa was the seal sign manual on Eastern Chalukya copper-plate seals. The royal emblem was the boar, the matronymic was Hariti-putra and the mother goddess was Hariti.

old: Vimaladitya bore the title Rajamartanda; Chalukya Bhima was Kollabhiganda, Saktivarma I Chalukya Chandra and Rajaraja Narendra Rajarajanarayana.
new: Rajamartanda (also Mummadi Bhima) was a title of Vimaladitya. Saktivarma I was Chalukya Chandra, Rajaraja Narendra was Rajarajanarayana, and Kollabhiganda was Vijayaditya IV, not Chalukya Bhima.

old: Rajaraja Narendra was crowned in 1022 CE; Saktivarman I defeated Satyasraya in 1006 CE and Vijayaditya VII was ousted in 1070 CE.
new: Rajaraja Narendra was crowned on 16 August 1022. In 1006 Saktivarma I defeated Bayyalanambi (sent by Satyasraya), and in 1070 Vijayaditya VII ousted Rajendra Chalukya.

old: Vijayaditya II is traditionally said to have fought 108 battles in 12 years. The 108 temples were commemorative constructions associated with these victories.
new: Vijayaditya II is said to have fought 108 battles in 12 years. He built 108 Saiva temples as penance for these battles, as recorded in the Sataluru inscription.

old: Nannaya composed the Nandampudi inscription, which records the agrahara granted to his collaborator Narayana Bhattu under Rajaraja Narendra. Trap: the APPSC G2 2017 key marked Nannaya as the donee, so know both. Pandaranga is linked to Addanki and Ugradityacharya to Kalyanakaraka.
new: Nannaya composed the Nandampudi inscription of Rajaraja Narendra, and the agrahara was given to his collaborator Narayana Bhattu (G2 2017 key). Pandaranga is linked to the Addanki inscription and Ugradityacharya to Kalyanakaraka.

old: The 2025 key makes Ayyana Mahadevi the queen of Kubja Vishnuvardhana. Some sources say Gunaga Vijayaditya III, but the key disagrees. Ammaraja II is linked to Chamekamba and the Kaluchumbarru grant; Vimaladitya married Kundavai.
new: The standard view (Musinikonda grant) makes Ayyana Mahadevi the queen of Kubja Vishnuvardhana; note that the APPSC 2025 key gave Gunaga Vijayaditya III. Ammaraja II is linked to Chamekamba and the Kaluchumbarru grant, and Vimaladitya married Kundavai.

old: The Eastern Chalukyas called themselves Haritiputras and their mother goddess was Hariti (APPSC G2 2019); Kushmandini is a Jain yakshi. Kalyanakaraka is Ugradityacharya's medical treatise, not a Shaiva school, and the leading Jain centre was Potlacheruvu.
new: The Eastern Chalukyas called themselves Haritiputras and their mother goddess was Hariti (APPSC G2 2019); Kushmandini is a Jain yakshi. Kalyanakaraka is Ugradityacharya's medical work, not a Shaiva school.

old: By using Telugu in royal and legislative records, the Renati Cholas gave it royal dignity about five centuries before Nannaya. (A match could not be built honestly from this single fact, so it is a one-liner.)
new: The Renati Cholas were the first to make Telugu a royal and legal language, replacing Prakrit and Sanskrit, about five centuries before Nannaya.

old: Tikkana was minister and court poet of Manumasiddhi II and sought Kakatiya Ganapati's help against Vijayaganda Gopala.
new: Kavi-Brahma Tikkana was the minister and court poet of the Nellore Choda Manumasiddhi II. When Manumasiddhi II sought Kakatiya Ganapati's help against Vijayaganda Gopala, Tikkana went as envoy.

old: The Velanati line ended when Kakatiya Ganapatideva killed its last member (named in some sources as Prithvisvara).
new: The Velanati Choda line ended when Kakatiya Ganapatideva killed its last member, Mummadi Rajendra Choda. Earlier, the Nellore Choda Tikkana had helped Ganapati kill Prithvisvara.

old: The Kalyani Chalukyas ruled from about 973 CE, when Tailapa II overthrew the Rashtrakutas, to 1195 CE. 543–753 CE is the Badami Chalukya period.
new: The Kalyani Chalukyas ruled from 973 CE, when Tailapa II overthrew the Rashtrakutas, to about 1189 CE, so the first option is the closest. 543–753 CE is the Badami Chalukya period.

old: The Anaimangalam (Leiden) plates, ordered by Rajaraja I and engraved under Rajendra I, were returned on 16 May 2026 during the PM's visit.
new: On 16 May 2026 the Netherlands returned the Anaimangalam (Leiden) copper plates at The Hague. They were ordered by Rajaraja I, engraved under Rajendra I and extended by Kulottunga I.

old: Narthamalai paintings show Shiva and Parvati; Chola murals are also known at Gangaikondacholapuram, with fine Dakshinamurthy panels at Thanjavur.
new: The Chola-period paintings at Narthamalai show Shiva and Parvati. Chola murals are also found at Gangaikondacholapuram.

old:
Singhana II, who ruled from 1200 to 1247, was regarded as the greatest Yadava ruler and bore the title ‘Teluguraya Sthapanacharya’.
⚠ Sources differ: Singhana II's reign is given as 1200-1247 in some sources and c.1210-1246 in others. This key follows the notes.
new: Singhana II (c. 1210–1246) was the greatest Yadava ruler. He bore the title Teluguraya Sthapanacharya, 'installer of the Telugu king'.

old: The Yadava court poet Hemadri claimed that Jaitugi captured and sacrificed Kakatiya Rudra.
new: Hemadri, the Yadava minister and scholar, claimed that Jaitugi captured and sacrificed the Kakatiya Rudra.

old: Ganapatideva built the Lakkavaram and Ghanapur tanks; Kesamudram was Prola I's and Arikesari Samudram Prola II's.
new: Ganapatideva built the Lakkavaram and Ghanapur tanks. The Kesari (Arikesari) Samudram, also called Kesamudram, was built by Prola I.

old: Marco Polo visited Motupalli c. 1287–1290 in Rudrama's reign and praised the ruling queen.
new: Marco Polo visited the Kakatiya port Motupalli (Mutfili) c. 1292–93, in Rudrama's reign, and praised the ruling queen.

old: Prasadaditya of the Kayastha family bore Kakatiya Rajya Sthapanacharya and helped Rudrama to the throne; Recherla Rudra was Bharadhureya.
new: Prasadaditya of the Recherla family bore the titles Kakatiya Rajya Sthapanacharya and Raya Pitamahanka. Recherla Rudra was Kakatiya Rajya Bharadhureya.

old: The Kazipet inscription, associated with Betha Raju II (Durgaraja), records Durga Nripathi coming to the throne.
new: The Kazipet (Dargah) inscription of Beta II and Durgaraja records the accession of Durga Nripathi (Durgaraja) and gifts to the Betesvara temple.

old: Rudra Deva acceded in 1158 and Kumaragiri Reddy in 1386. 1296 is the accession of Pratapa Rudra, not Durga Nripathi.
new: Rudra Deva came to the throne in 1158 (Draksharama inscription) and Kumaragiri Reddi in 1386, so 1 and 2 are correct. Durgaraja (Durga Nripathi) ruled 1108–1116, not from 1296, so 3 is wrong.

old: Mummadi Nayaka built the Pakhala tank; Prola II built Arikesari Samudram, Recherla Rudra the Ramappa tank and Ganapatideva Laknavaram.
new: Mummadi Nayaka, son of Bayyana Nayaka, built the Pakhala tank. Prola I built the Kesari (Arikesari) Samudram, Recherla Rudra the Ramappa tank and Ganapatideva the Laknavaram tank.

old: The recorded principle (cited from Ketana's Vijnaneswaramu and Purushartha Saramu) was that a woman's property passed to her daughters and daughter's daughters, a comparatively progressive outlook.
new: Ketana's Vignaneswaram (the Telugu Mitakshara) says a woman's property passes wholly to her daughters and daughter's daughters, a progressive legal outlook. Purushartha Saramu is a different work, on the 72 Niyogas.

old: The order is Rudradeva (1158), Mahadeva, Ganapatideva, Rudramadevi (1260), Prataparudra (1296).
new: The order is Rudradeva (1158), Mahadeva, Ganapatideva, Rudramadevi (1262) and Prataparudra (1296), so Mahadeva came between Rudradeva and Ganapatideva.

old: The Tanisha Mahal palace stands at the far end of Kondapalli fort, between two hills.
new: The Tanisha Mahal palace stands inside Kondapalli fort, between two hills; the main gate is the Dargah Darwaza.

old: Muhammad Shah I burned Kapaya's son Vinayaka alive in 1361. Orugallu was subdued by Mahmud Gawan, Ahmad Shah I moved the capital to Bidar, and Gawan was executed in 1481 or 1482 according to the differing dates cited.
new: Muhammad Shah I burned Kapaya's son Vinayaka alive in 1361. Orugallu was subdued by Muhammad III and Mahmud Gawan (not Firoz Shah), Ahmad Shah I shifted the capital to Bidar, and Mahmud Gawan was executed in 1481.

old: The terms included a marriage alliance, the Balakrishna idol, and return of lands north of the Krishna to the Gajapati. Permanent annexation of all Gajapati territories south of the Krishna was not stated.
new: The peace terms were the marriage of Prataparudra's daughter to Krishnadevaraya, the gift of the Balakrishna idol and the return of lands north of the Krishna to the Gajapati, who stayed as a feudatory. Cuttack and the Gajapati heartland were NOT taken over.

old: Andhra Shabda Chintamani is the first Telugu grammar in Sanskrit; Ganita Sara Sangraha is the first Telugu mathematics book.
new: Andhra Shabda Chintamani, ascribed to Nannaya, is a Telugu grammar written in Sanskrit. Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam (Ketana) is the first grammar written in Telugu, Ganita Sara Sangraha is Mahaviracharya's mathematics work, and Kavyalankara Chudamani (Vinnakota Peddana) is the first alankara work.

old: Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Bengal for the Ghurids after taking Bihar and destroying Nalanda and Vikramshila.
new: Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji entered Nadiya in 1204, drove Lakshmana Sena to East Bengal and ruled from Lakhnauti, after conquering Bihar.

old: Newly built temples were ordered to be destroyed, though court music bans coexisted with Persian works on Indian music.
new: Under Aurangzeb, newly built temples were ordered to be destroyed. His 1669 order led to the demolition of the Kashi Vishwanath and Keshava Rai (Mathura) temples.

old: Haq-i-sharb was one-tenth; his canals carried water from the Yamuna and Sutlej to Hisar.
new: Firoz Shah's irrigation cess, haq-i-sharb, was one-tenth of the produce. He built the largest number of canals among the Delhi Sultans.

old: Option C is incorrect: Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504, not Delhi. Razia as the only woman Sultan, Firoz Shah's canals and Muhammad bin Tughluq's token currency are right.
new: Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504, not Delhi, so this statement is incorrect. Razia was the first and only woman ruler, Firoz Shah is known for canals, public works and Ashokan pillars, and Muhammad bin Tughluq introduced token currency and moved the capital to Daulatabad.

old: Sultan Garhi was built by Iltutmish as the tomb of his son Nasiruddin Mahmud. The Red Palace was Balban's palace, the Jamat Khana Masjid was built by Alauddin Khalji, and Firoz Shah Kotla was Firoz Tughlaq's citadel at Firozabad, so the other pairs are wrong.
new: Sultan Garhi was built by Iltutmish as the tomb of his son Nasiruddin Mahmud. The Red Palace (Kushk-i-Lal) was Balban's palace, the Jamat Khana Masjid was built by Khizr Khan, son of Alauddin Khalji, and Firoz Shah Kotla was Firoz Tughlaq's citadel of Firozabad, so the other pairs are wrong.

old: The silver rupiya was standardised by Sher Shah at 178 grains, and Akbar continued it. Option B gives the wrong weight (106 is the Koh-i-Noor's carats); option C names Tughlaq, known for token currency; option D confuses the 40 dams to a rupee.
new: Sher Shah fixed the silver rupiya at 178 grains, and Akbar continued it. Forty copper dams made one rupee.

old: Muslin, saltpetre, indigo and sugar were exports. The other groups contain goods listed as imports.
new: Muslin, saltpetre, indigo and sugar were all exports of Mughal India. Each of the other groups contains imports such as watches, tin, ivory, glass, copper, war horses, silver, porcelain and wine.

old: Humayun's tomb was the first garden tomb in the subcontinent; it used red sandstone with white marble inlay and introduced the double dome.
new: Humayun's tomb was the first garden tomb in the subcontinent. It used red sandstone with white marble inlay and had the first full Persian double dome in Mughal architecture.

old: The Dutch network in Andhra extended from Machilipatnam in the south-western part of the network to Bheemunipatnam in the north-east.
new: The Dutch network in Andhra ran from Machilipatnam to Bheemunipatnam, along the coast.

old: Yayati Charitra is identified as the first kavya in pure Telugu. Its dedication is attributed to Amir Khan in one account and to Ibrahim in another.
new: Ponnaganti Telaganarya's Yayati Charitra was the first kavya in pure (achcha) Telugu. He dedicated it to Amir Khan, Ibrahim Qutb Shah's governor of Patancheru.

old: The correct sequence is Mudgal in 1358, Goa’s loss in 1472, the capture of Gulbarga in 1523, and Talikota in 1565.
new: The correct order is: Bukka I took Mudgal (1367), Goa was lost to the Bahmanis (1472), Krishnadevaraya took Gulbarga (1523), and the Battle of Talikota was fought (1565).

old: Ibn Battuta is listed as the first foreign traveller, in Harihara I's reign. Nicolo Conti came under Devaraya I/II, Abdur Razzaq under Devaraya II (1443) and Domingo Paes under Krishnadevaraya.
new: Ibn Battuta was the first foreign traveller to visit, in Harihara I's reign. Nicolo Conti came under Devaraya I, Abdur Razzaq under Devaraya II (1443) and Domingo Paes under Krishnadevaraya.

old: Abdali's repeated invasions occurred during Alamgir II's reign.
new: Punjab and Multan were ceded to Ahmad Shah Abdali in the reign of Alamgir II (1754-1759), during Abdali's repeated invasions.

old: Afanasy Nikitin was a Russian traveller from Tver, situated on the Volga. He visited Vijayanagara during the reign of Virupaksha Raya II.
new: Afanasy Nikitin was a Russian horse merchant from Tver on the Volga. He visited the Bahmani kingdom under Muhammad Shah III (from 1469).

old: Qutbuddin Aibak began the Qutb Minar and dedicated it to Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.
new: The Qutb Minar, begun by Aibak and completed by Iltutmish, is dedicated to the Sufi saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.

old: It was issued by Bhaskara Mantri and records the Anantasagaram tank (1369, Bukka I's time), not by Krishnadevaraya.
new: The Porumamilla inscription, with its 12 rules (Dwadasa Sutras) for building a tank, was issued by Bhaskara (Bhaskara Bhavadura), son of Bukka I and prince of Udayagiri. It records the Anantasagaram tank (1369) in Kadapa; it was not issued by Krishnadevaraya.

old: Lepakshi dates to about the 1530s, in Achyutaraya's reign; the Tungabhadra location belongs to the Virupaksha temple.
new: The Lepakshi temple was built c. 1530-40 by the Nayaka brothers Virupanna and Veeranna of Penukonda, officers of Achyutaraya, so it belongs to Achyutaraya's reign.

old: Tazkiras are biographies of saints. Anti-Shia tracts are represented by works such as ‘Radd-i-Khawafiq’.
new: Tazkiras are biographies of saints, not anti-Shia tracts. Malfuzat are conversations and Maktubat are letters. Radd-i-Rawafiz, an anti-Shia tract, was written by Ahmad Sirhindi.

old: The amin made the revenue assessment in Sher Shah's system. The shiqdar, qanungo and patwari were also revenue/local officials; none of them prepared manuscripts, commanded the cavalry or minted coins, so B, C and D are false pairs.
new: The amin (munsif) of the pargana made the revenue assessment. The shiqdar kept law and order, and the qanungo and patwari kept revenue and local records; none of them prepared manuscripts, commanded the cavalry or minted coins.

old: Baji Rao I's ideology was Hindu Pad Padshahi, aimed at striking the Mughal centre.
new: Baji Rao I's ideology was Hindu Pad Padshahi. His slogan "strike the trunk, the branches will fall" meant striking at the Mughal centre.

old: The grant was Rs 1,00,000 (1 lakh) a year, the first step towards State responsibility for education; Rs 10 lakh is a misprint.
new: The Charter Act of 1813 gave Rs 1,00,000 (1 lakh) a year for education. It was the first step towards State responsibility for education.

old: The commonly cited distribution gave the state 10/11 of the rent collected and the zamindar 1/11. Some accounts mention a 9/10 and 1/10 division, but the cited assessment here uses 1/11.
new: Under the Permanent Settlement the State took 10/11 of the rent collected and the zamindar kept 1/11.

old: The Mahalwari-type arrangement is placed in Nellore (with Chittoor in some accounts); Vizianagaram and Bobbili were zamindaris under the Permanent Settlement.
new: Nellore had a Mahalwari-type arrangement, where village headmen collected and paid the tax. Vizianagaram and Bobbili were zamindaris under the Permanent Settlement, paying peshkash.

old: Large foodgrain imports and inflation led the First Plan to give top priority to agriculture, irrigation and power. Post-partition stabilisation was another immediate challenge.
new: Large foodgrain imports and inflation after independence led the First Plan to give top priority to agriculture, irrigation and power.

old: Osmania University was founded by Mir Osman Ali Khan in 1917–18, not 1930; the other dates are correct.
new: Osmania University was founded by Mir Osman Ali Khan in 1918, not 1930. The other dates are correct: Nizam College 1887, Noble's school at Machilipatnam 1843 and Madrasa-e-Aliya 1873.

old: Warren Hastings founded the Calcutta Madrasa (1780); Fort William College was Wellesley's, the Asiatic Society was Jones's and Hindu College was Ram Mohan Roy's and David Hare's.
new: Warren Hastings founded the Calcutta Madrasa in 1781. Fort William College was founded by Richard Wellesley, the Asiatic Society by William Jones, and Hindu College by Ram Mohan Roy and David Hare.

old: Lord Mayo undertook a statistical survey of India and conducted the first census (1871).
new: Besides financial decentralisation (Resolution of 1870), Lord Mayo undertook a statistical survey of India and held the first census in 1872.

old: Satara (1848) was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. Jhansi lapsed in 1853 and Nagpur later. Awadh (1856) was annexed for misgovernment, not under lapse.
new: Satara (1848) was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse; Jhansi and Nagpur followed in 1854. Awadh (1856) was annexed for misgovernment, not under lapse.

old: Rani Lakshmibai’s adopted son, Damodar Rao, was not recognised as heir and Jhansi was annexed in 1853.
new: Rani Lakshmibai's adopted son, Damodar Rao, was not recognised as heir, so Jhansi was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in 1854 (the Raja had died in November 1853).

old: Only 1 is correct: Mubariz-ud-Daula was imprisoned before Turrebaz Khan's attack; the Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula stayed pro-British.
new: Only statement 2 is correct: Mubariz-ud-Daula was imprisoned in Golconda before Turrebaz Khan's attack on the Residency. Statement 1 is wrong because Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula stayed pro-British.

old: The phrase “breakwaters to the storm” is attributed to Lord Canning, although some accounts credit Lord Elgin.
new: Lord Canning called the loyal princes "breakwaters to the storm", because they kept their states quiet and helped the British during the revolt.

old: Lord Canning described the loyal princes as breakwaters to the storm, though some accounts credit Lord Elgin.
new: Lord Canning called the princes who stayed loyal in 1857 "breakwaters to the storm".

old: Veeresalingam founded it at Rajahmundry in 1878 (APHQ 2019), and K. Seethamma later organised its women's wing. Machilipatnam, Guntur and Visakhapatnam were not the site of the first centre.
new: Kandukuri Veeresalingam founded the first Prarthana Samaj in Andhra at Rajahmundry in 1878 (APPSC 2019). K. Seethamma later organised its women's wing.

old: 'Prophet of Indian Nationalism' is a title of Swami Vivekananda; the others belong to Dayananda.
new: Lala Lajpat Rai called Dayananda the 'Martin Luther of India'; he is also called the 'Grandfather of the Indian Nation' and is credited with first using the term Swaraj. 'Prophet of Indian Nationalism' is a title of Swami Vivekananda, not Dayananda.

old: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in 1875. David Hare and Raja Ram Mohan Roy are linked with Hindu College, and Alexander Duff with the Scottish mission college.
new: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded it at Aligarh: it began in 1875 as a school (Madarsatul Uloom Musalmanan-i-Hind) and was renamed the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College in 1877.

old: Mahmud-ul-Hasan gave Deoband political content; Shibli Numani founded the Nadwat al-Ulama at Lucknow and wanted English and European science taught.
new: Mahmud-ul-Hasan gave the Deoband movement political content, which led to the Jamiat-ul-Ulema. Shibli Numani backed Deoband but wanted English and European science taught.

old: Rajahmundry and Kakinada were the main Brahmo centres in Andhra, where the movement peaked during 1870–1935.
new: Rajahmundry and Kakinada were the main centres of the Andhra reform movement, which peaked in 1870-1935. Kakinada, with its Brahma Mandir, was also Venkataratnam Naidu's Brahmo centre.

old: Option B is incorrect: Veeresalingam started Satihita Bodhini in 1883, not 1886. Vivekavardhini (1874), Satyasamvardhini (1891) and Brahma Prakasika (1886) are right.
new: Satihita Bodhini was started by Veeresalingam in 1883, not 1886, so B is the incorrect statement. Vivekavardhini (1874) and Brahma Prakasika (1886, Venkataratnam Naidu) are right, and Satyasamvardhini did begin in 1891.

old: Andhra Prakasika was the first Telugu political weekly; Chintamani (1891) is called the first Telugu political journal.
new: Andhra Prakasika, started by A.P. Parthasarathi Naidu in 1885, was the first Telugu political weekly. It is also counted as the first Telugu political journal; Chintamani (1891) came later.

old: Musalamma Maranamu was written by Gurajada Apparao, not Tripuraneni Gopichand. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
new: Musalamma Maranamu was written by Kattamanchi (C.R.) Ramalinga Reddy, not Tripuraneni Gopichand, so this pair is wrong. Veyi Padagalu is by Viswanatha Satyanarayana, Gabbilam by Gurram Jashuva and Kanyasulkam by Gurajada Apparao.

old: The Female Infanticide Act of 1870 was associated with Lord Mayo. Lansdowne was associated with the Age of Consent Act, Irwin with the Sarda Act, and the 1872 Native Marriage Act had no Governor-General specified in the table.
new: The Female Infanticide Prevention Act of 1870 was passed under Lord Mayo, so B is correct. The Age of Consent Act (1891) was under Lansdowne and the Sarda Act (1929) under Irwin; the Native Marriage Act (1872) was passed at Keshab Chandra Sen's urging, not under Canning.

old: Warren Hastings was Governor-General from 1772 to 1785 and his tenure included the Rohilla War, the First Anglo-Maratha War and the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
new: Warren Hastings was Governor of Bengal from 1772 and Governor-General from 1774 to 1785. His time included the Rohilla War (1774), the First Anglo-Maratha War and the Second Anglo-Mysore War.

old: Salbai was 1782; Madras 1769, Allahabad 1765 and Bassein 1802.
new: The Treaty of Salbai was signed in 1782. The Treaty of Madras was 1769, the Treaty of Mangalore 1784 and the Treaty of Bassein 1802.

old: The Rampa rebellion began with the attack on Chintapalli police station on 22 August 1922 and effectively ended with Alluri Sitarama Raju's death at Koyyuru on 7 May 1924.
new: The Rampa rebellion ran from August 1922 to May 1924, about 1 year 9 months. It began with the attack on Chintapalli police station on 22 August 1922, and Raju was shot at Koyyuru on 7 May 1924.

old: Kavi Samrat is Viswanatha Satyanarayana; Rayaprolu is Abhinava Nannaya.
new: Kavi Samrat is Viswanatha Satyanarayana, not Rayaprolu, so B is not correct. Rayaprolu is the Father of Telugu Romanticism and wrote Andhravali; some lists also call him Abhinava Nannaya, though the APPSC G2 2025 key gave that title to Viswanatha.

old: Kalluru Subbarao donated the land; the Parishad was inaugurated by the Governor on 11 February 1956.
new: Kalluru Subbarao gave the land for the Lalita Kala Parishad, Anantapur, which was set up on 11 February 1956.

old: T. Varalakshmamma presided at Devarakonda in 1931; the 1938 Madras Andhra Mahila Sabha was a separate body founded by Durgabai Deshmukh.
new: T. Varalakshmamma chaired the Devarakonda conference (1931) of the Andhra Mahila Sabha of the Nizam's Andhra Mahasabha. It was separate from the Andhra Mahila Sabha of Madras founded by Durgabai Deshmukh.

old: The Mughal firman granting the Circars to the East India Company was issued by Shah Alam II in 1765, though some sources date it to 1766.
new: Shah Alam II's Mughal firman of 1765, received by Clive, granted the Northern Circars to the Company. Nizam Ali refused it at first and leased the Circars only in 1766.

old: Robert Clive secured the firman from Shah Alam II; the firman is dated 1765 in the detailed chronology.
new: Robert Clive secured the firman for the Northern Circars from the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II in August 1765.

old: The All Parties Muslim Conference at Delhi in January 1929, presided over by the Aga Khan, rejected the Nehru Report.
new: The All Parties Muslim Conference met at Delhi from 31 December 1928 to 1 January 1929 under the Aga Khan. It rejected the Nehru Report and demanded separate electorates.

old: Sayyid Ahmad Khan, along with Raja Shiv Prasad of Bhinga, promoted an anti-Congress front in 1887.
new: In 1887-88 Lord Dufferin used Sayyid Ahmad Khan as an anti-Congress front, along with Raja Shiva Prasad of Benares and the Raja of Bhinga; the United Indian Patriotic Association followed in 1888.

old: Harijan was started in 1933 (January 1933 in some sources), with the first issue from Poona. 1919 is when Gandhi began editing Young India; 1903 at Durban is Indian Opinion; 1936 is the founding of Sevagram at Wardha.
new: Harijan weekly brought out its first issue on 11 February 1933 at Poona. 1919 is when Gandhi began editing Young India; 1903 at Durban is Indian Opinion; 1936 is the founding of Sevagram at Wardha.

old: The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, or Majoor Mahajan Sangh, was founded in 1920 by Anusuya Sarabhai with Gandhi’s guidance.
new: The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association (Majoor Mahajan Sangh) was founded by Gandhi with Anusuya Sarabhai on 25 February 1920; it worked through arbitration and non-violence.

old: The failure of the Cripps Mission (March 1942), which offered no immediate self-government, was the immediate trigger for Quit India. Gandhi called the Cripps offer a 'post-dated cheque' (Nehru is credited with adding 'on a crashing bank'). Shimla 1945 and the INA's 1943 revival came later, and the 1939 ministry resignations were only background.
new: The failure of the Cripps Mission (March 1942), which offered no immediate self-government, was the immediate trigger for Quit India; Gandhi called the Cripps offer a 'post-dated cheque'. The Simla Conference (1945) and the INA's revival (1943) came later, and the 1939 ministry resignations were only background.

old: Its mandate was to identify the financial and administrative problems of forming Andhra State (PYQ, APPSC G2 2012); its March 1953 report fixed the new state's districts. Statewide linguistic reorganisation was the SRC's task, the Andhra-Madras border the Pataskar Award's, and Telangana safeguards came from the 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement.
new: The Wanchoo Committee, appointed in December 1952 after Potti Sriramulu's death, was asked to identify the financial and administrative problems of forming Andhra State (APPSC G2 2012); it reported on 7 February 1953. Linguistic reorganisation of all states was the SRC's task, the Andhra-Madras border was settled by the Pataskar Award, and Telangana safeguards came from the 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement.

old: Urdu was retained for five years (then reviewed by the Regional Council), not ten.
new: Under the Gentlemen's Agreement, Urdu was to be kept in Telangana's administration and courts for five years, and then reviewed.

old: He called the post a 'sixth finger'; this breach fed the grievances behind the 1969 Jai Telangana movement.
new: Neelam Sanjiva Reddy appointed no Deputy CM, calling the post a 'sixth finger'.

old: Andhra Prakasika was edited by A.C. Parthasarathi Naidu; Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu edited Brahma Prakasika.
new: Andhra Prakasika was edited by A.P. Parthasarathi Naidu, not Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu; Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu edited Brahma Prakasika. Golconda Patrika (Suravaram Pratap Reddy) and Desamata (Chilakamarti Lakshmi Narasimham) are correctly matched.

old: Vijnana Chandrika Mandali was founded by Komarraju Venkata Lakshmana Rao at Hyderabad in 1905 (APHQ says 1906), not at Vijayawada. The other pairs are correct: Andhra Saraswati Parishad (Hyderabad, 1922), C.V.N. Granthalayam (Ongole, 1890), Andhra Council of Research (Kovvur, 1916).
new: Vignana Chandrika Mandali was founded by Komarraju Lakshmana Rao at Hyderabad in 1906, not at Vijayawada. The other pairs are correct: Andhra Saraswati Parishad (Hyderabad, 1922), C.V.N. Granthalayam (Ongole, 1890) and Andhra Council of Research (Kovvur, 1916).

old: Prasad was elected on 11 December 1946, not at the first meeting, which was attended by 211 members and boycotted by the Muslim League.
new: Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946. The first meeting on 9 December 1946 had 207 members and was boycotted by the Muslim League.

old: The Muslim League called Direct Action Day as a protest against Wavell inviting the Congress to form the Interim Government. It was followed by the Calcutta riots.
new: The Muslim League called Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946 to press for Pakistan after it withdrew from the Cabinet Mission Plan. It led to the Calcutta riots.

old: Mypadu was in Nellore; Chinnapuram was near Machilipatnam and Devarampadu near Ongole.
new: Mypadu (spelt Mylapadu beach in the notes) is in Nellore district, where Bezawada Gopal Reddy made salt. Devarampadu, the 'Dakshina Dandi', was near Ongole.

old: Kanneganti Hanumanthu was shot dead during the cattle-rescue action at Minchalapadu on 26 February 1922.
new: Kanneganti Hanumanthu was shot dead in the cattle-rescue action at Minchalapadu on 22 February 1922. The cattle had been impounded there; Macherla was where officials were socially boycotted.

old: The order was Jai Telangana (1969), Jai Andhra (1972), 32nd Amendment (1973), GO 610 (1985) and Girglani Report (2004).
new: The 32nd Amendment was enacted in 1973, along with the Six-Point Formula. It inserted Articles 371D and 371E and came into force on 1 July 1974.

old: Kaka Kalelkar chaired the First National Backward Class Commission; he is not a figure of modern Dalit assertion in AP.
new: Kaka Kalelkar chaired the First Backward Classes Commission, set up in January 1953 under Article 340; it reported in 1955. The Second Commission was chaired by B.P. Mandal.

old: The anti-arrack movement began in Dubagunta (Nellore) in 1991, led by rural women from the Aksharajyothi literacy classes, and is regarded as one of India's most successful women-led movements.
new: The anti-arrack movement began in 1992 at Dubagunta village in Nellore district, led by rural women. It is regarded as one of India's most successful women-led movements.

old: Part IXA (Municipalities) covers Articles 243P-243ZG; Part IX covers 243-243O and Part IXB (Co-operative Societies, 97th Amendment, 2011) covers 243ZH-243ZT. No dated order can be built, so a one-liner is used.
new: Part IXA (Municipalities, added by the 74th Amendment, 1992) covers Articles 243P to 243ZG. Part IX (Panchayats) covers 243 to 243O and Part IXB (Co-operative Societies) covers 243ZH to 243ZT.

old: The AP-specific reference identifies the 32nd Amendment Act of 1973 as having inserted Articles 371D and 371E relating to the Six-Point Formula and the Central University. A conflicting reference to the 33rd Amendment is ambiguous and is not the applicable identification here.
new: The 32nd Amendment Act, 1973 inserted Article 371D (the AP Six-Point Formula on public employment and education) and Article 371E (a Central University in Andhra Pradesh). It was the 32nd, not the 33rd.

old: Potana offered the work to Lord Rama, not to Krishnadevaraya (a sequence cannot be built as the facts carry no dates).
new: Bammera Potana offered his Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu to Lord Rama, not to King Krishnadevaraya.

old: Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act provides that Aadhaar does not by itself prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth.
new: Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act says an Aadhaar number is not by itself proof of citizenship or domicile. It serves only for identity authentication and for benefits where the law requires it.

old: Sequence was not possible as the facts carry no dates. The President, as Supreme Commander, declares war and makes peace on the Council of Ministers' advice.
new: The President is the Supreme Commander of the Defence Forces. He declares war and makes peace on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

old: While acting as President, the Vice-President stops functioning as Chairman and the Deputy Chairman presides. (Sequence not possible: the facts carry no dates.)
new: While acting as President under Article 65, the Vice-President stops doing the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and the Deputy Chairman presides.

old: Vemavarapu Ramadasu Pantulu moved the separate-province resolution. Konda Venkatappayya was the secretary and is also associated with the reception committee; B.N. Sarma was the president.
new: Vemavarapu Ramadasu Pantulu moved the separate-province resolution at Bapatla (1913). Konda Venkatappayya was the secretary and B.N. Sarma was the president there, so the other pairs are wrong.

old: Nemali Pattabhirama Rao presided over the first session at Madras in 1934; the second, at Kadapa in 1935, was under K. Subrahmanyam.
new: Nemali Pattabhirama Rao presided over the first Rayalaseema Mahasabha at Madras (28 January 1934), not the second. The second session, at Kadapa in September 1935, was presided over by T.N. Ramakrishna Reddy and opposed a separate Andhra state.

old: Suravaram Pratapa Reddy and Burgula Ramakrishna Rao founded the Jatiya Andhra Mahasabha. The other pairs mix coastal and Rayalaseema leaders.
new: Suravaram Pratapa Reddy and Burgula Ramakrishna Rao founded the Jatiya Andhra Mahasabha. Madapati Hanumantha Rao led the Andhra Jana Sangham (1921), and Ravi Narayana Reddy led the Communists at Bhongir (1944).

old: The Communists backed Vijayawada/Guntur; the Krishikar Lok Party backed Tirupati and the Congress Kurnool.
new: The Communists led by P. Sundarayya backed Vijayawada/Guntur as the capital. The Praja Socialist Party (not the Krishikar Lok Party) backed Tirupati, and the Congress backed Kurnool.

old: Per the original's explanation, the oath or affirmation (Third Schedule form) is made before the Election Commission or a person authorised by it.
new: Under Article 84, a candidate for Parliament must make an oath or affirmation, in the Third Schedule form, before a person authorised by the Election Commission.

old: The House would grow to about 815, and the 15% ministerial ceiling would rise from 81 to 122 (133 by another source).
new: Raising the Lok Sabha by about 50% after the 1971 freeze would take it to about 815 seats; the 15% cap on the Council of Ministers would then rise from 81 to 122.

old: The minimum age is 30 for the Council (Article 171) and 25 for the Assembly (Article 170).
new: Article 173 sets the minimum age for State legislators: 30 years for the Legislative Council and 25 years for the Legislative Assembly.

old: The 104th Amendment Act, 2020 ended Anglo-Indian nomination; the 106th (2023) provides about one-third reservation for women.
new: The 104th Amendment Act, 2019 (in force from January 2020) ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members under Article 333. The 106th Amendment (2023) provides about one-third seats for women.

old: Written as a one-liner (no dates for a sequence). The Council can only delay an Assembly Bill and cannot veto it; it is much weaker than the Rajya Sabha.
new: The Legislative Council can only delay an ordinary Bill passed by the Assembly (3 + 1 months) and cannot veto it. So its power is much weaker than that of the Rajya Sabha.

old: Article 246A gives Parliament and State Legislatures simultaneous power over GST; Panchayati Raj stays a State List subject.
new: Article 246A, inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016, gives Parliament and State Legislatures simultaneous power to make GST laws; only Parliament makes laws on inter-State supply.

old: Puttaswamy (2017) came after post-Emergency activism, the expansion of Article 21 and governance cases like 2G.
new: Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy as a fundamental right. It is a landmark of the later stage of judicial activism.

old: The Election Commission capped electors per polling station at 1,200 and delisted 808 RUPPs.
new: The ECI capped the number of electors per polling station at 1,200, down from the earlier 1,500.

old: Nine PSUs were given Navratna status and greater autonomy in 1997 (NCERT-based sources give 1996). 1991 is the year of the reforms, not of the Navratna scheme.
new: Nine PSUs were given Navratna status and greater autonomy in 1997. 1991 is the year of the reforms, not of the Navratna scheme.

old: A is true: under Article 243A, the Gram Sabha is all the voters on the village roll. R is false because the elected executive is the Gram Panchayat, not the Gram Sabha.
new: A is true: under Article 243(b) the Gram Sabha is the body of all persons registered as voters in the village electoral rolls. R is false: the elected executive body is the Gram Panchayat, not the Gram Sabha.

old: The triple test requires a dedicated commission, local-body-wise reservation on its findings and aggregate SC, ST and OBC reservation within 50 per cent. (Built as a one-liner: the facts carry no dates for a sequence.)
new: The Gawali triple test needs a dedicated commission with an empirical inquiry, local-body-wise reservation based on its findings, and total SC, ST and OBC reservation within 50 per cent.

old: Parliament passed the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Bill in December 2013, after the Bill's re-introduction in 2008.
new: Parliament passed the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Bill in December 2013: the Rajya Sabha on 17 December and the Lok Sabha on 18 December 2013. The President gave assent on 1 January 2014.

old: Section 11 requires an inquiry wing headed by a Director of Inquiry and a prosecution wing headed by a Director of Prosecution.
new: Section 11 of the Lokpal Act provides for the Inquiry Wing, headed by a Director of Inquiry; the Lokpal also has a Prosecution Wing headed by a Director of Prosecution. The other options name bodies that are not wings of the Lokpal.

old: Municipalities (and Nagar Panchayats) in AP are governed by the AP Municipalities Act, 1965, and Municipal Corporations by the AP Municipal Corporations Act, 1994 (as CDCA cites it; some 2026 reports name a 1955 Corporations Act). Options A and B swap or misdate the two Acts, and D names a Panchayats Act.
new: Municipalities and Nagar Panchayats in AP are governed by the AP Municipalities Act, 1965, and Municipal Corporations by the AP Municipal Corporations Act, 1994. Options A and B swap or misdate the two Acts, and D names a Panchayats Act.

old: PESA covers Scheduled Tribe populations constituting approximately 8.6 percent of India's population.
new: As per Census 2011, Scheduled Tribes form about 8.6 percent of India's population, spread over 705 notified groups.

old: Option C is incorrect: under Article 281, the President, not the Finance Minister, has the Finance Commission's report laid before both Houses, with a note on action taken.
new: Under Article 281 the President, not the Finance Minister, causes the Finance Commission report to be laid before both Houses of Parliament, with an explanatory memorandum on action taken. The other statements are correct.

old: The 1872 Act, also called the Native Marriage Act, provided monogamous civil marriage and prohibited child marriage.
new: The Special (Civil) Marriage Act, 1872 was also called the Native Marriage Act. It provided a monogamous civil marriage, with ages of 14 for the girl and 18 for the boy.

old: Bigamy is BNS Section 82 (old IPC 494-495); IPC marriage offences are now BNS Sections 81-84.
new: Bigamy (old IPC Section 494) is now BNS Section 82; the IPC marriage offences (Sections 493-498) are now BNS Sections 81-84.

old: Inter-caste conflicts are now mostly about power rather than ritual status, and caste dominance rests increasingly on secular factors (no dates, so not a sequence).
new: Inter-caste conflicts today are mostly about power, not ritual status, and caste dominance now rests on secular factors.

old: The Act was enacted in 1987; 2001 marked the National Policy for Empowerment of Women.
new: The Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, which bans sati and its glorification, was enacted in 1987. 1829 is the Bengal Sati Regulation, 1961 the Dowry Prohibition Act and 1986 the Indecent Representation of Women Act.

old: Statement 1 is correct: IBSA was founded in 2003 by the Brasilia Declaration. Statement 2 is wrong: the IBSA Trust Fund (operational 2004, funds LDC projects) is managed by UNOSSC, not UNDP. Statement 3 is correct: IBSAMAR is the IBSA naval exercise. So 1 and 3 only (B); A misses statement 3, C and D include statement 2.
new: Statement 1 is correct: IBSA was founded in 2003 by the Brasilia Declaration. Statement 2 is wrong: the IBSA Trust Fund (working from 2004, funds LDC projects) is run by UNOSSC, not the World Bank. Statement 3 is correct: IBSAMAR is the IBSA naval exercise, so the answer is 1 and 3 only.

old: C. Rangarajan chaired the 2012 committee on poverty measurement. Tendulkar (2005) came before it, and Hashim and Saxena (2009) dealt with BPL lists and rural poverty.
new: C. Rangarajan chaired the Rangarajan Expert Group (set up 2012, report 2014). Suresh Tendulkar chaired the earlier 2005 group, while S.R. Hashim (urban BPL households) and N.C. Saxena (rural BPL census) headed the 2009 groups.

old: GANHRI accredits national human-rights institutions ('A' for fully compliant, 'B' for others), based on independence and effectiveness.
new: GANHRI accredits national human-rights institutions through its Sub-Committee on Accreditation: 'A' means fully and 'B' partly compliant with the Paris Principles.

old: Iran executed at least 2,159 people in 2025, followed by Saudi Arabia (356+); China's figure is a state secret and not counted.
new: Amnesty's 2025 report recorded Iran as the top executioner with at least 2,159 executions, followed by Saudi Arabia. China is not counted because its figures are a state secret, though it remains the biggest executioner.

old: The Accessible India Campaign is Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan; UDID comes under Social Justice and Empowerment.
new: The Accessible India Campaign is also called Sugamya Bharat Abhiyan. It was launched on 3 December 2015 as the flagship of DEPwD.

old: After decline in 1911–1921 came the Great Divide in 1921, the explosion of 1961–1971 and high but slowing growth in 1981–2011.
new: 1921 is called the Great Divide: population declined in 1911-21 and grew steadily after 1921. The explosion phase was 1951-81 (over 2% a year), and 1981-2011 saw high but slowing growth.

old: The NCM Act does not define 'minority'; a community notified by the Centre is a minority for the Act, though States may notify their own for State purposes.
new: Under Section 2(c) of the NCM Act, a minority is any community notified by the Central Government. States may also name their own minorities for State purposes.

old: The Act does not define minority; under Section 2(c) a minority is any community notified by the Central Government. Section 3(2) requires five members including the Chairperson to be from minority communities; Article 29(1) protects the language, script or culture of any section of citizens; Section 9(1) of the Waqf Act, 1995 concerns the Central Waqf Council.
new: Under Section 2(c) of the NCM Act, 1992, a minority means any community notified by the Central Government. Article 29(1) protects the language, script or culture of any section of citizens, and Section 9 of the Waqf Act, 1995 concerns the Central Waqf Council.

old: The legal heir of a deceased consumer may file a complaint, and the right is not confined to free medical services.
new: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the legal heir of a deceased consumer may file a complaint in his or her place.
